subtype: Approach: seeking advice from an older sibling [Action]
passage: Preeti found her brother Jagdish at the far table of the school canteen, where the Class 12 boys ate. "Five minutes," she said. She told it fast: Reema had repeated the name of a boy Preeti liked to the whole bench, and Preeti never wanted to speak to her again. Jagdish chewed slowly. "When did you last reply to her?" "That's not the point." "Preeti." A pause. "Last Tuesday," she admitted. "She sent three messages after that." Jagdish nodded. "I did this to Vikram in ninth. I went quiet, he blurted my business to prove he mattered, and we both lost a term." It stung, but Preeti knew it was fair. "So I talk to her first?" "Say what hurt. And say you went quiet too."

qa.a: Preeti found Jagdish at the far table of the school canteen.

qa.q: How does Preeti feel on hearing that her silence may have played a part?
qa.a: Preeti feels stung but accepts it, because she knows Jagdish's point is fair.

qa.q: What approach could Preeti take with Reema, and why?
qa.a: Preeti could ask for a quiet chat, say what hurt and admit she went quiet too, because that opens listening on both sides.

qa.q: How might Reema have felt when her messages went unanswered?
qa.a: Reema may have felt dropped and ignored, hurt enough to lash out by repeating the name.

grounding: The student explains the situation to her elder brother, who has been through similar fights, and gets a reality check that helps her see her own part in the misunderstanding.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from an older sibling [Action]
passage:
Baljeet Bhaiya,
Thanks for picking up at eleven last night. I know I cried through half the call. I've been thinking about what you said. I told you Simran ditched me for the new girl and "didn't even care". You asked, "Did you tell her you wanted to come?" I said she should have known. Then you told me about you and Harman in Class 11, how you stopped talking for a month because each of you waited for the other to guess. That was hard to hear. Because honestly, I never told Simran I felt left out. I just went cold and made sarcastic comments at lunch. Maybe she thinks I dumped her. I'm going to talk to her tomorrow, properly this time, and say my part too.
Your little sister,
Nikita

qa.q: What time did Baljeet Bhaiya pick up?
How did Nikita feel when Baljeet asked whether she had told Simran?
qa.a: She felt defensive at first, insisting Simran should have known, then uncomfortable once the story about Harman showed her own part.

qa.q: Why was talking to an older brother helpful here?
qa.a: He had been through similar fights and could gently point out that she never told Simran how she felt, which a friend on her side might not do.

qa.q: How might Simran have seen Nikita's cold behaviour?
qa.a: Simran may have read it as Nikita dumping her, not knowing Nikita felt left out.

grounding: A student's letter to her elder brother shows how his reality check helped her see her own part in a misunderstanding with a friend.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from an older sibling [Action]
passage: Ankita, just listen for a minute, okay? It's Yamini, and I'm not calling to fight. After Saturday I was so angry that I went to my brother, Kartik Bhaiya. He's twenty and he's had about fifty fights with his best friend, so I thought he'd take my side. I told him you cancelled our movie for your cousin and didn't even say sorry. He listened, then asked, "Did you tell her the movie mattered because it was your results day?" I hadn't. He said, "Then she cancelled a movie. You thought she cancelled you." That stung. And he said the snapping on the chat afterwards was on me, not you. So I'm sorry for snapping. And the movie did matter, because of my results. Can we go next week?

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when the brother's question landed?
qa.a: Yamini felt stung and a bit embarrassed, realising the reason the movie mattered had never been said.

qa.q: What makes Yamini's call a good next step?
qa.a: Yamini owns the snapping, explains why the movie mattered and suggests a new plan, so Ankita hears both the apology and the real feeling.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel hearing the call?
qa.a: Ankita may feel surprised and relieved, finally understanding why the cancellation hurt, and glad the fight is ending.

grounding: A student tells a friend how an elder brother's reality check showed the speaker's own part in their misunderstanding.
